date_enacted: Town Board voted 6-1 on July 21, 2026 to approve an ordinance introduced by Mayor Jamie Jeffery.

Over 400 residents petitioned via an Action Network campaign organized by the nonprofit 'With Many Hands,' citing water and electricity concerns amid statewide drought.
current_status: Previously reported active as of 2026-09-23. Ordinance 2026-720 was adopted July 21, 2026 for five years from its effective date, subject to earlier termination or extension; subsequent current force has not been independently established in this review.
affected_projects: The mayor told Rocky Mountain PBS that no data-center developer had approached Lochbuie about building in town; the report identifies the proposed Cielo Hudson Data Center in neighboring Hudson.
outcome: Town Board adopted Ordinance 2026-720 by a 6-1 vote, imposing a five-year moratorium on covered data center applications from its effective date, subject to earlier termination or extension. The pause was reported as the longest such pause in Colorado.

duration: 180 days as adopted; the data center, battery and solar components were rescinded effective February 17, 2026, and the wind component was rescinded effective April 7, 2026.

All four facility types covered by Resolution 2025-25 were superseded by their own permanent regulation resolutions, each with an explicit rescission clause tied back to Resolution 2025-25: Resolution 2026-4 (Battery Energy Storage Systems, effective 2026-02-17), Resolution 2026-5 (Data Center Facilities, effective 2026-02-17), Resolution 2026-6 (Solar Energy / Community Solar Garden, effective 2026-02-17), and Resolution 2026-11 (Wind Energy Facilities, adopted 2026-04-07, shortly before the moratorium's own ~2026-04-19 lapse date). Commissioner Yahn noted the moratorium had already been planned before this specific proposal surfaced. As of a January 2026 hearing, commissioners stated no formal permit application had yet been received.

affected_projects: None named; Loveland had not received a formal data center application as of adoption, though the city acknowledged informal developer interest.
outcome: City Council approved a 12-month suspension on large-scale data center development applications while staff develop permanent land use regulations.

The Citizen Portal account attributed rescission of a previous 2024 measure; its precise relationship to the March 2025 action remains unverified. The recovered records do not establish a lapse beginning June 30, 2025.

The Zoning Commission had not yet formally recommended a permanent ordinance.

No final county ordinance had been adopted as of the captured March 17, 2026 zoning commission meeting.

Town Counsel Donna MacNicol told voters before the vote that the BESS portion was unlikely to survive Attorney General review because standalone BESS is treated as a protected/solar-adjacent use under G.L. c. 48, Section 3, and recommended splitting the article into two motions; voters instead approved the combined article as written (several Massachusetts towns, including Blandford, Worthington, and Wendell, had similar BESS moratoria disapproved by the AGO's Municipal Law Unit in 2026). No Attorney General Municipal Law Unit decision specific to this Gill bylaw was located as of 2026-09-23. The Gill Planning Board's Sept. 17, 2026 meeting agenda lists 'Review Data Centers for bylaw updates,' consistent with continuing work toward permanent regulations during the moratorium period.

Separately, in an unrelated case (a resident-led environmental-justice challenge to MassDEP's air permits for the facility), a Superior Court judge paused Markley's installation of four new diesel backup generators on 2026-08-10; that litigation was ongoing as of 2026-09-23.

The standards set noise limits (noise-producing equipment generally at least three-quarters of a mile from an occupied home), require closed-loop cooling, and set setback, water/power-use, road, emergency-planning, and reclamation-bond requirements (with a waiver path if a former data center site is repurposed). legal_basis: Order of Austin County, Texas, Regarding Battery Energy Storage Systems and Data Centers Health and Safety Review, adopted by the Commissioners Court on 2026-07-27 under Texas Health and Safety Code section 121.003 and Texas Local Government Code section 352.016, among other authorities. The signed, executed order was located directly on austincounty.com (distinct from the earlier unsigned draft). It suspends county permit, plan-review, and inspection approvals for BESS and data center construction in unincorporated areas until a 'Comprehensive Health and Safety Review' (covering fire/life-safety, cybersecurity/foreign-adversary equipment verification tied to the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act and the Governor's Prohibited Technologies List, and an Energy Development Zone siting study) is complete, with the Commissioners Court retaining sole discretion over when that review is finished. It requires County Fire Marshal plan review/approval and an independent third-party engineering evaluation before construction, and authorizes the County's legal counsel to seek injunctive relief against violators.
trigger: Comprehensive health and safety review of AI data centers and battery energy storage systems
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Commissioners Court unanimously adopted the signed order on 2026-07-27 following the July 13, 2026 public hearing; KWHI (2026-07-28) independently confirms the unanimous vote and describes the order's scope (equipment-manufacturer audits, an Energy Development Zone siting study by the County Fire Marshal and County Engineer, and injunctive-relief enforcement authority). No fixed term applies; the order remains in effect, by its own terms, until the Commissioners Court (in consultation with the County Fire Marshal) determines the Comprehensive Health and Safety Review is complete. No repeal, rescission, or completion of the review was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. KWHI notes Austin County is 'the second county in Texas to adopt a moratorium of this nature,' after Hill County (which later rescinded its moratorium following a developer lawsuit; see the existing tx-hill-county-2026 row).

duration: Two years from adoption, as an interim zoning bylaw
legal_basis: Interim zoning bylaw adopted unanimously by the Morristown Select Board and Village of Morrisville Board of Trustees, dated 2026-08-31, following a selectboard proposal and two public hearings in August 2026
trigger: Town bylaws are silent on data centers and 'high-impact uses'; board wants time for the planning commission to study electric-grid, water, noise, and hazardous-waste impacts before any application is filed, prompted in part by community reaction to a separate large industrial-park/quarry proposal
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The interim zoning bylaw (dated 2026-08-31) blocks consideration of applications for data centers and other defined 'high-impact uses' -- facilities that consume 10+ megawatts of power from any source, use 57,600+ gallons of water per day, discharge hazardous waste, add more than 10 acres of impervious surface, or emit more than 70 decibels of persistent noise -- for two years, with an exemption for small data centers necessary for the administrative/operational support of an existing business, hospital, school, municipal service, or residence. Intended to give the planning commission time to draft permanent zoning addressing such uses; runs through approximately 2028-08-31.
affected_projects: None named; officials and residents confirmed no data center has been proposed in Morristown and few parcels are large enough to host one, but the board called the moratorium precautionary.
outcome: Adopted unanimously by the Select Board and Village Board of Trustees on 2026-08-31 after a public hearing with dozens of residents, most supportive; Morristown is the third Vermont community (after Royalton's permanent five-year ban and South Burlington's zoning amendment) to restrict data centers.

date_enacted: 2026-07-21 (City Council adopted Resolution 26-R-042 by a 9-0 vote)
duration: 8 months from adoption, or until City Council takes final action on comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002, whichever occurs first
legal_basis: Resolution 26-R-042, adopted by Chesapeake City Council 9-0 on July 21, 2026
trigger: Council sought to pause discretionary review of data center land-use applications while comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002 is pending
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Resolution 26-R-042 deferral remains in force, running 8 months from its July 21, 2026 adoption (to approximately 2027-03-21) or until Council takes final action on comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002, whichever occurs first. On August 18, 2026 the City Council separately and unanimously adopted a zoning ordinance amendment that requires a conditional use permit for data centers across the city except within Coastal Virginia Commerce Park (CoVAC), where the city says data centers may still be built by-right, and prohibits data centers from drawing groundwater; this closed a loophole that could have let a data center proceed administratively despite the moratorium, but it is a permanent zoning change layered on top of, not a replacement for, the still-active Resolution 26-R-042 deferral. The zoning change was prompted partly by Praetorian Fund's August 2026 purchase of the Frank Williams Farm Tract (Coastal Virginia Commerce Park); because that site does not connect to public utilities, city officials confirmed the moratorium independently applies to it. No repeal, extension, or expiration of the moratorium itself was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: No single named project; applies citywide to discretionary data center land-use applications pending before the Planning Commission or City Council.
outcome: Enacted deferral of discretionary data center land-use applications pending completion of a related comprehensive plan amendment.

legal_basis: Board motion approving a moratorium on new data center applications; related resolution of intention and ZTA 25:10
trigger: Data centers were by-right uses in I-1 and I-2 districts, and the Board directed staff to prepare amendments requiring special use permits.
current_status: Replaced / expired for the 2025 moratorium, as previously recorded; a local report says the Board approved the special-use zoning change on 2025-12-17. A separate August 2026 report describes a later pause through December 31 while a further zoning change was considered; it is a distinct action.
affected_projects: No named project or MW total identified in the captured packets; contemporaneous rezoning comments raised concern about possible data center use.
outcome: ZTA 25:10 moved data centers from by-right use to special use permit treatment in I-1 and I-2 and modified the data center definition.

date_enacted: 2026-07-06, Front Royal Town Council work session, 6-0 vote (Vice Mayor Amber F. Veitenthal and Councilmembers DeDomenico-Payne, Ingram, Rappaport, Sealock, and Wood; Mayor Cockrell present but votes only to break ties), per the town's own approved council minutes.
duration: 90-day administrative moratorium adopted 2026-07-06; council extended it by an additional 60 days on 2026-09-28. The exact final end date and effect of the later zoning action remain unverified.
legal_basis: Resolution Establishing a Temporary Ninety (90) Day Moratorium on the Acceptance of Data Center Land Use Applications, adopted 6-0 by Front Royal Town Council at its July 6, 2026 work session. Town Attorney George Sonnett advised the moratorium was structured as an administrative action (rather than a legislative zoning-ordinance amendment) because, in his opinion, Virginia law does not authorize a legislative moratorium through the zoning ordinance.
trigger: The town sought to preserve the status quo while it drafts a permanent zoning text amendment to define data centers separately from 'technology' uses and prohibit data centers in all town zoning districts; no data center application had been received as of adoption.
current_status: The 90-day application moratorium adopted 2026-07-06 was extended by 60 days on 2026-09-28. Local news reports the council unanimously adopted a zoning text prohibition on 2026-10-26, after the September work-session review. Whether that action terminated the administrative moratorium and its exact end date remain unresolved.
affected_projects: None named; Town Manager Joseph Petty confirmed no data center applications had been received as of the July 6, 2026 vote.
outcome: Front Royal Town Council adopted a 90-day administrative moratorium on data center land-use applications while it drafts a permanent zoning prohibition.

date_enacted: 2026-09-15, Loudoun County Board of Supervisors vote, as reported in its September 16 release; the base pause and grid-reliability exception each passed 7-1-1.
duration: The September 15 immediate pause was tied to Phase 2 of the Data Center Standards and Locations initiative. A formal resolution proposed a limit of 12 months from each application’s first submission to the Planning Commission; its October 20 consideration was deferred to November 17.
legal_basis: September 15, 2026 Board action, described in the county’s September 16 release as an immediate pause on consideration of certain legislative applications with a grid-reliability exception. The October 20 proposed formal resolution was deferred; its proposed per-application limit and retroactive language are not treated as adopted. Grandfathered administrative cases were reported unaffected. The prior record attributes to the County Attorney that Virginia law does not permit a blanket moratorium on administrative applications and reports roughly 17 grandfathered cases totaling more than 11 million square feet under the March 2025 resolution.
trigger: Regulatory gap and community pressure over rapid data center growth in the county ("Data Center Alley"); effort led by Algonkian District Supervisor Juli Briskman, tied to the county's ongoing Phase 2 Data Center Standards and Locations initiative (begun September 2025) addressing data center/substation siting, noise, building heights, on-site power generation, and battery storage standards.
current_status: The county’s September 16 release reports that the Board voted 7-1-1 on September 15 for an immediate pause on certain legislative data center and substation applications during Phase 2, with a separate 7-1-1 grid-reliability exception. It reports grandfathered administrative cases are unaffected. On October 20 a formal resolution with a proposed 12-month per-application limit was deferred to November 17, according to October 21 reporting; this does not establish repeal of the earlier action. Current legal effect and scope remain qualified pending primary confirmation. The earlier record attributes the separate exception vote opposition to Supervisor Briskman and reports that the Board was to receive legal analysis on October 6 concerning grandfathered cases without vested rights.
affected_projects: At least 17 land-use cases representing more than 11 million square feet of data center development are 'grandfathered' under the county's March 2025 resolution and continue through by-right administrative review, unaffected by this pause.
outcome: Loudoun County reported an immediate pause on Board consideration of certain legislative data center and substation applications during its Phase 2 review, subject to applicable deadlines and a grid-reliability exception. A later proposed formal resolution was deferred.

The official package contains a proposed ordinance; the final adopted text, effective date, duration and later legal status remain unverified. [VERIFY adopted instrument, effective date, duration and subsequent action]

date_enacted: 2026-08-18, Virginia Beach City Council, unanimous vote.
duration: 12 months from adoption, or until City Council takes final action on an ordinance regulating data centers, whichever occurs first (to approximately 2027-08-18).
legal_basis: Resolution adopted by Virginia Beach City Council on August 18, 2026, pausing the issuance of permits related to any new data center for 12 months or until Council takes final action on an ordinance regulating data centers, whichever occurs first; follows planning staff's finding that data centers are currently classified, by default, as wholesaling/warehousing/storage/distribution uses permitted by right in industrial districts.
trigger: City zoning ordinance does not specifically define or regulate data centers; concerns raised over resource consumption (water, electricity), noise, and land-use compatibility, following an informal June 2026 Council statement opposing large-scale/hyperscale data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Virginia Beach City Council unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data center permits on August 18, 2026, the same night Chesapeake City Council closed its by-right loophole. The moratorium does not affect existing facilities such as Globalinx's subsea-cable colocation operations, and is intended to apply to future larger-scale and hyperscale data center proposals while the city studies zoning definitions, setbacks, and noise standards. No repeal, extension, or replacement ordinance was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: No large-scale storage/computing data center currently operates in Virginia Beach; existing subsea-cable landing and carrier-neutral colocation facilities (e.g., Globalinx) are not affected.
outcome: Virginia Beach City Council unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data center permits while it develops zoning definitions and regulations for the industry.

date_enacted: 2026-03-03 (interim zoning controls prohibiting BESS citywide, Ordinance No. 26-1246, superseding an earlier BESS permit-application moratorium first adopted 2024-02-15 under Ordinance No. 24-1205 and renewed by Ordinance No. 25-1219 in February 2025); extended a further six months, with a small-system exception, by Ordinance No. 26-1258 (public hearing scheduled 2026-10-06)

date_enacted: 2018-10-17 (Spokesman-Review reported the "City Council voted Wednesday" of 2018-10-17 to block new cryptocurrency operations for 12 months; vote 6-1 with Mayor Reim absent)

Note: EMC 19.02's definition of 'high intensity computer operations' expressly excludes the exchange of cryptocurrency/virtual currency and peer-to-peer distributed-ledger maintenance, so the permanent code is framed as a broader high-density-computing-load prohibition rather than a cryptocurrency-specific one.

affected_projects: Four existing cryptocurrency operations were reported (two at the Port of Ephrata, one in a city-zoned industrial area, and one in a residential area being relocated); the moratorium applied to new operations only
outcome: The temporary 2018 cryptocurrency-mining moratorium was followed, within the same year, by a permanent zoning prohibition on high-intensity computer operations (EMC Chapter 19.30), citing Ordinance 18-13 and Ordinance 18-28, confirmed via the current Ephrata Municipal Code (Title 19, Zoning Code).

legal_basis: Seattle Ordinance 127447 (Council Bill 121214), Sections 2-3: citywide moratorium on filing, acceptance, processing or approval of applications to establish, expand or change use to data centers, as principal or accessory uses. Section 2 exempts expansions of no more than an additional 20 MVA at facilities operating on the effective date that meet the definition or would meet it except for existing capacity at or below 20 MVA. current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Vilas County Zoning & Planning Committee held a public hearing on the proposed ordinance on 2026-09-23 (the date of this research); the full County Board of Supervisors is scheduled to vote at its October 27, 2026 meeting. As drafted, the moratorium would freeze acceptance, review, or approval of development permits for data centers, BESS, and solar energy systems that exceed one acre (the acreage threshold applies to solar systems only), for 12 months, with exemptions for solar installations of one acre or less, ordinary maintenance/repairs, emergency utility restoration, and projects already holding valid county permits. Subsequent September 25 reporting states that the committee voted unanimously to recommend the proposal on September 23 and that a full-board vote was scheduled for November 10, 2026; this conflicts with the earlier October 27 schedule and the board outcome is unverified. The report also describes proposed changes involving home solar and battery backups; final exemptions remain unverified.
outcome: Public hearing held on a proposed 12-month moratorium on data centers, battery energy storage systems, and solar energy systems over one acre (the acreage threshold applies to solar systems only); County Board vote scheduled for 2026-10-27. September 25 reporting says the committee unanimously recommended the proposal and expected a November 10 board vote; final board action remains unverified.
